sub: Technology block (a): describing every interface in the UTM diagram

title: What Is OpenAPI?
desc: A specification for describing RESTful APIs — machine-readable, human-friendly

items: OpenAPI is a specification for describing RESTful APIs
Enables a standardized definition of API endpoints and their functions
Originally developed as Swagger, now governed under the Linux Foundation (OpenAPI Initiative)
Standardization — uniform API documentation across teams and vendors
Automatic generation — code, documentation and test cases generated from the spec
Interactive use — try APIs live, e.g. in Swagger UI
Easier API design — collaboration between developers and stakeholders on one artifact
A NOTAM service, a METAR service (Module 12), a UTM clearance service — all of them need exactly this kind of contract

title: Anatomy of an OpenAPI Document
desc: APIs are described in YAML or JSON — five top-level building blocks

body.code: openapi: 3.1.0 info: title: UTM Flight Clearance API version: 1.0.0 servers: - url: https://utm.example.com/v1 paths: /drones/{droneId}/clearance: post: summary: Request flight clearance for a mission responses: '201': { description: Clearance granted } '409': { description: Conflict with another mission }

items: openapi — version of the specification, info — metadata: title, version, description
servers — available servers, paths — definition of the API endpoints
components — reusable schema definitions (e.g. a Mission object shared by several endpoints)
Use 3.1 for new work: its schemas are plain JSON Schema, and every generator supports it today

title: The Course Contract: telemetry.yaml
desc: The one interface every project touches — the Android client posts a fix, the backend accepts it

body.code: openapi: 3.1.0 info: { title: Drone Telemetry API, version: 1.0.0 } paths: /drones/{droneId}/fixes: post: summary: Ingest one position fix from the Android client (M5) parameters: - { name: droneId, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: string } } requestBody: required: true content: application/json: schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/Fix' } responses: '202': { description: Accepted — published to telemetry.topic (M9) } '422': { description: Rejected — altitude above 120 m or timestamp in the future } components: schemas: Fix: type: object required: [lat, lon, altMeters, ts] properties: lat: { type: number, minimum: -90, maximum: 90 } lon: { type: number, minimum: -180, maximum: 180 } altMeters: { type: number, minimum: 0, maximum: 120 } ts: { type: string, format: date-time }

items: Fix is the same object Module 9 publishes on the topic and Module 14 draws on the map — one schema, three modules
The unit is in the name (altMeters) — the Module 2 rule, applied at the API boundary
422 turns the open-category ceiling into a contract rule: the server refuses what the law forbids — and Module 11 tests exactly that response

title: From Spec to Code: Generate Both Ends
desc: Spec-first — the YAML is the source of truth, client and server are derived from it

body.code: # Kotlin client for the Android app (M5) openapi-generator-cli generate -i telemetry.yaml -g kotlin -o client/ # Spring WebFlux server stub (M8) openapi-generator-cli generate -i telemetry.yaml -g spring \ --additional-properties=reactive=true -o server/ # Swagger UI served by the running service (build.gradle.kts) implementation("org.springdoc:springdoc-openapi-starter-webflux-ui:2.8.0")

body.card: What you get — and what you still write
items: Generated: a typed client (TelemetryApi.postFix(droneId, fix)), the server interface with routes and DTOs, and the Fix class on both sides — the same object the app sends and the server validates
Yours: the handler body (publish to the topic), and any rule the schema cannot express — e.g. this drone has no clearance for this zone

body.card: Two ways to get a spec
items: Spec-first: write the YAML, generate the code — this course, because the Android client (M5) and the Karate tests (M11) are built from the same file
Code-first: annotate Spring controllers, let springdoc emit the YAML — quick for one team, drifts as soon as a second consumer appears
Either way: never edit generated code — change the spec, regenerate

title: OpenAPI Tooling: Swagger Editor & Friends
desc: One spec, a whole toolchain — live demo in the editor

items: Swagger UI — visual rendering and in-browser test calls (try the live editor)
Redoc — modern, read-oriented API documentation
Postman — API testing and development
OpenAPI Generator — client/server code generation for dozens of languages

body.alt: Swagger Editor with the Petstore example: YAML on the left, rendered documentation with GET/POST endpoints on the right
body.caption: Try it yourself at editor.swagger.io — paste the Petstore example, or telemetry.yaml from two slides ago.

items: OpenAPI describes a REST API as a single machine-readable contract — humans and tooling read the same artifact
From that one spec you generate documentation, client and server code — and Module 11 derives the tests from it
Spec-first: the YAML is the source of truth; generated code is never edited, only regenerated
telemetry.yaml is the course's contract: the Fix schema travels unchanged from the Android app (5) through the topic (9) to the map (14)
